title: First Responder Presumptive Laws
text:
ALERRT Center · Texas State University




Cancer. Heart disease. PTSD. First responders face these at higher rates than the general population — but getting workers’ compensation often means proving your job caused it. Presumptive laws shift that burden, treating these illnesses as work-related by default. Coverage varies widely across all 50 states.

Open the Coverage Map →

title: First Responder Presumptive Laws
text:
What is a presumptive law?
Under standard workers’ compensation rules, a sick first responder must demonstrate that their specific job directly caused their illness — a nearly impossible bar for diseases like cancer or heart disease that develop over years. A presumptive law eliminates that requirement: the illness is presumed to be work-related, and the burden falls on the employer to prove otherwise.
Most presumptions are rebuttable — the employer can present contradicting evidence. A small number are irrebuttable, meaning the link is conclusive regardless of other evidence. Coverage also depends on which conditions are listed in the statute, which occupations qualify, how many years of service are required, and whether there’s a post-retirement window.

Keeping track of where these protections exist — and what they actually cover — is harder than it should be. The Coverage Map is an attempt to fix that.

title: First Responder Presumptive Laws
text:
How to use this app


01 Pick a mode. Use Occupation to ask which conditions are covered for a specific responder type. Use Condition to ask which states cover a specific illness — and for whom.


02 Read the chart. The intersection diagram shows how many states cover each combination of responder groups. Hover a bar to see which states; click to lock the selection.


03 Click the map. Selecting a state opens a detailed table of all laws on record — statute citations, service requirements, post-employment coverage, and notes.


04 Verify before acting. Laws change. Always confirm current status with a qualified attorney or your state’s workers’ compensation board.

About this project
The Coverage Map was developed by the ALERRT Center at Texas State University. ALERRT conducts applied research on first responder training, health, and wellness.
This dashboard is built from original research conducted directly against each state’s statutory text — not a repackaging of any single outside source. The IAFF Presumptive Health database was used as a starting point for where to look, but every entry here was traced back to, and verified against, the actual law. See the About page for full methodology and citation.
Prototype This is an early-stage research tool. If you notice an error or a law that has changed, the About page explains how to interpret the data.

title: About
text:
Primary source Original legislative research — direct review of primary statutory text, all 50 states
Every entry in this dashboard is based on a dedicated research pass against the actual law: official state code websites, state legislature bill-tracking pages, and reputable full-text legal mirrors (public.law, Justia, FindLaw). Each state’s statute citations, covered conditions, covered occupations, service requirements, and effective dates were traced from the primary text itself, not copied from a secondary summary. Every state write-up then went through an independent second review before being added to the dashboard.


Starting-point reference IAFF Presumptive Health database — iaff.org/presumptive-health
Maintained by the International Association of Fire Fighters, this database was used as an initial lead on where to look in each state — a directory to check, not a source to trust outright. Comparing it against the primary statutory text repeatedly turned up problems: wrong statute citations, outdated effective dates, missing conditions, and mischaracterized benefit types. Where IAFF’s page and the actual law disagreed, this dashboard follows the law.


Cross-check reference Neugent, K., & Spidell, B. (2023). Firefighters and first responders: 2023 update on presumptive workers comp benefits. National Council on Compensation Insurance (NCCI).
Covers approximately 38 NCCI-jurisdiction states; data current through November 2022. Used to cross-check IAFF data for covered states during initial extraction.


Cross-check reference Brandt-Rauf, S., Davis, A. L., & Taylor, J. A. (2024). Inventory of state workers’ compensation laws in the United States: first responder mental health. Journal of Public Health Policy, 45, 562–574.
50-state inventory using the Westlaw legal database; data current through December 2022. Used to supplement IAFF data for mental health / PTSD coverage, which is less consistently documented in other sources.

title: About
text:
Methodology
For each state, a dedicated research pass identified the governing statute(s) directly from primary sources — official state code sites, state legislature bill pages, and full-text legal mirrors — and traced amendment history and effective dates from that text. IAFF’s page for the state was checked only as a starting hypothesis about where to look; it was not treated as the final word. Law attributes — condition covered, occupations covered, statute citation, service requirements, post-employment coverage, and restrictions — were then coded into a structured dataset from the verified primary text. Each row represents one state × condition category × occupation combination.
Each completed state write-up went through an independent second review focused on accuracy and completeness before being added to the dashboard. This process found IAFF’s page to be wrong, stale, or incomplete for a substantial number of states — citing the wrong statute, using outdated effective dates, omitting conditions or restrictions, or mischaracterizing what type of benefit a law provides — and this dashboard’s entries reflect the corrected, source-verified version rather than IAFF’s characterization.
Where the primary statutory text itself is ambiguous about whether a provision is historical or currently active, that uncertainty is reflected in the data. A small number of entries are flagged with * in the Notes column where the active status of a statute is genuinely unclear from the law itself.

Data currency: This dashboard reflects a point-in-time research pass, completed August 2026. Laws change. Always verify current status with a qualified attorney or your state’s workers’ compensation board before relying on this resource for legal or financial decisions.
